slides.title: Definitions as Biconditionals
slides.html:
Definitions as Biconditionals

I can test whether a definition is a good one by checking both directions.

geo.title: Definitions as Biconditionals
geo.target: I can test whether a definition is a good one by checking both directions.

slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Each group writes a definition of 'kite.' Another group tries to find a shape that fits the definition but isn't a kite, or a kite that doesn't fit. (Agree first: does a rhombus count as a kite?)

  • I can test whether a definition is a good one by checking both directions.
  • I can write a definition as an 'if and only if' statement.
  • I can test a definition by hunting for counterexamples in both directions.

geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Each group writes a definition of 'kite.' Another group tries to find a shape that fits the definition but isn't a kite, or a kite that doesn't fit. (Agree first: does a rhombus count as a kite?)

  • I can test whether a definition is a good one by checking both directions.
  • I can write a definition as an 'if and only if' statement.
  • I can test a definition by hunting for counterexamples in both directions.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A good definition works in both directions, so it can be written with 'if and only if.' It must let in every example and keep out every non-example. Course rules: 'isosceles' means at least two equal sides, and a rhombus counts as a kite.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: A good definition works in both directions, so it can be written with 'if and only if.' It must let in every example and keep out every non-example. Course rules: 'isosceles' means at least two equal sides, and a rhombus counts as a kite.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• biconditional ('if and only if') A statement where the conditional and its converse are both true.
  • definition An exact meaning. Every good definition works as an 'if and only if' statement.
  • example A case that fits the definition.
  • non-example A case that does not fit the definition, which helps show its edges.
  • counterexample One example that makes a statement false.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Test a definition of rectangle.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Test: 'a rectangle is a quadrilateral with at least one right angle.'A definition must keep out every non-rectangle.
Take a quadrilateral with angles 90, 60, 120 and 90 degrees.These angles are given.
It has a right angle, but it is not a rectangle. The test lets in a non-example.One shape breaks the definition.
Better: a quadrilateral is a rectangle if and only if it has four right angles.This states both directions at once.
Second check: every rectangle has four right angles, and every quadrilateral with four right angles is a rectangle. The 90, 60, 120, 90 shape is now kept out.Both directions hold.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Fix a test for 'balanced' triples.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
A triple of integers is 'balanced' when two numbers are positive and one is zero.This is the definition.
Proposal: a triple is balanced if and only if its sum is positive.Test both directions.
(1, 1, 1) has a positive sum but no zero, so it is not balanced.The proposal lets in a non-example.
Fix: balanced if and only if one number is zero and the other two are positive.This matches the definition exactly.
Second check: (0, 2, 3) passes and (1, 1, 1) fails.The right triples get in, and the wrong one stays out.

Proposal: a triple is balanced if and only if its sum is positive.
(1, 1, 1) has a positive sum but no zero, so it is not balanced.
steps.reason: The proposal lets in a non-example.

steps.step: Fix: balanced if and only if one number is zero and the other two are positive.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Gus defines a kite as "a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides." A counterexample is a parallelogram ABCD with these given lengths: AB=CD=a and BC=DA=b, where a and b are positive and unequal. It passes Gus's test. But every adjacent pair has one side of length a and one of length b, so it has no equal adjacent pair and is not a kite.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

Correct definition: the four sides can be grouped into two disjoint pairs, with the sides in each pair adjacent and equal. The lengths of the two pairs need not differ, so a rhombus counts as a kite. (In plain words: A kite's four sides must split into two pairs, using each side once. In each pair, the two sides meet at a corner and have equal lengths. The lengths of the two pairs may be the same, so a rhombus counts. The given parallelogram is not a kite because its neighboring side lengths a and b are positive and unequal.)

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Test this definition: 'the midpoint of AB is a point M that is the same distance from A and B.' Then fix it.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

It lets in too much: a point P off the segment can have PA = PB, and P is not a midpoint. Fix: M is the midpoint of AB if and only if M is on segment AB and AM = MB.

Reveal second check

Check both ways: every midpoint is on AB with AM = MB, and any point like that is the midpoint. P is now kept out, because it is not on AB.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
A definition says a square is a shape that 'looks nearly square.' Why can't that define squares, even if every example shown looks right?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

'Nearly' has no exact cutoff, and looks are not measurements. Use the exact definition: four equal sides and four right angles.

Reveal second check

A 1 by 1.001 rectangle looks square when it is small, but its sides are not equal.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
'An acute angle is an angle whose measure is less than 90 degrees.' In our course, angles go from 0 to 180 degrees. What case slips through?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

It lets in 0 degrees. Fix: an acute angle has a measure more than 0 and less than 90 degrees.

Reveal second check

The fixed test keeps out 0 and 90 and lets in 45. The old test let in 0.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
Split 'a triangle is equilateral if and only if all three sides are equal' into two if-then statements.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

If a triangle is equilateral, then all three sides are equal. If all three sides of a triangle are equal, then it is equilateral.

Reveal second check

Name the given, measurement, assumption, definition or proof you used.
